claude.sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

links.outcome: Hallucinations in LLM-generated EHR summaries rated by radiologist experts
links.effect: Mean expert hallucination scores (0–1 scale, 1 = hallucination present) ranged 0.60–0.90 across the six summarizing models, indicating frequent hallucinated content.

links.outcome: Agreement of LLM-as-a-Judge with expert reference standard for hallucination detection
links.effect: Kendall's W for hallucination detection was 0.37–0.55 across judges and prompt configurations; authors conclude LLM judges are not advisable for detecting hallucinations in semantically difficult medical text.
links.quote: Our results indicate that it is not advisable to use LLM-as-a-Judges to search for hallucinations in texts, especially when analyzing a semantically difficult medical text.

links.outcome: Consistency of LLM judge scores for the same summary across scale sizes and prompt granularities
links.effect: The same summary got 3/4, 4/5, 6/7 and 4/10 completeness from Mistral; inconsistency more pronounced at larger scales; often three different scores across three prompt granularity variants.
links.quote: When reviewing the responses of LLMs-as-a-Judges, periodic inconsistencies in scores assigned to the same summary across different scale granularities became apparent.

links.outcome: Disagreement among radiologist experts defining and grading summary quality
links.effect: Experts disagreed on task requirements based on clinical profile, modality and institutional school; consensus of three experts used for ground truth.
links.quote: However, even at the task formulation stage, we encountered disagreements among the experts.

unlisted_practices: Tuning LLM-as-a-judge rating scale size and prompt granularity to maximize agreement with expert raters
Involving diverse end-user expert teams and a cognitive scientist to define evaluation criteria for LLM judges
Using language-specific fine-tuned judge models (T-Pro 2.0 outperformed base Qwen3-32B in Russian)

openai.sample_unit: LLM-generated clinical summaries from 30 patient EHRs

links.outcome: automatic metric validity for medical summaries
links.effect: ROUGE-1 0.29–0.38, BLEU 0.06–0.12, BERTScore 0.72–0.77; authors judged automated metrics poorly applicable.
links.quote: The results presented in Table 4 indicate that automated metrics are poorly applicable to our task.

links.outcome: LLM-judge score stability across rating scales
links.effect: Mistral scored the same summary’s completeness 3/4, 4/5, 6/7, and 4/10 across scale sizes.
links.quote: For example, the LLM-as-a-Judge Mistral evaluated the completeness of Summary №10 as follows: 3 out of 4 points, 4 out of 5 points, 6 out of 7 points, and 4 out of 10 points.

links.outcome: clinically significant omissions in AI summaries
links.effect: Expert Completeness averaged 3.26/5 while Grammar and Terminology averaged 4.4/5.
links.quote: Therefore, in our experiment, experts rated the summarizations with relatively high scores according to the criterion of Grammar and Terminology (on average 4.4 out of 5) but with substantially lower scores according to the criterion of Completeness (on average 3.26 out of 5).

links.effect: Kendall W for hallucination detection was 0.37–0.55 across models/prompt detail; authors advised against LLM-as-Judges for semantic hallucinations.
links.quote: In general, all models showed rather low consistency with experts, which indicates the weak ability of LLM to detect semantic hallucinations in medical texts.

unlisted_practices: Configuring LLM-as-a-judge rating scale size for clinical summary evaluation
Choosing prompt granularity for LLM-as-a-judge scoring
Using locally trained or local-language LLMs as judges for Russian clinical text

links.outcome: Completeness and hallucinations in LLM-generated clinical summaries
links.effect: Experts rated LLM summaries lower on completeness (average 3.26 out of 5) and detected frequent hallucinations (model averages 0.60–0.90), despite high grammar and terminology scores (average 4.4 out of 5).
links.quote: Therefore, in our experiment, experts rated the summarizations with relatively high scores according to the criterion of Grammar and Terminology (on average 4.4 out of 5) but with substantially lower scores according to the criterion of Completeness (on average 3.26 out of 5).
